name: Gluteal tendinopathy (greater trochanteric pain syndrome)

diagnosisContested.note: Partly contested. The condition is accepted, but GTPS is a non-specific umbrella term covering bursitis, external snapping hip and gluteus medius/minimus tendinopathy or tears. There is no consensus on the most useful clinical tests. Tendon changes on MRI were found in 88% of asymptomatic women in one small study, so imaging correlates poorly with symptoms. Trials used varying eligibility criteria. Kinsella 2024 (6 studies, 272 people, certainty very low to moderate) found that in people with lateral hip pain, positive gluteal tendon palpation followed by positive resisted abduction raised the probability of GTPS from 59% to 96%, and both negative lowered it to 14%. ISHA 2023 names gluteal tendinopathy with or without bursitis as the primary pain source, and the NHS Lothian fact sheet calls MRI findings a poor predictor of symptoms.

avoidOrModify.movement: Stretches that pull the hip into adduction, such as iliotibial band stretches and piriformis or glute stretches that draw the knee across the body
avoidOrModify.rationale: These positions combine compression of the tendons against the greater trochanter with passive tensile load, and the LEAP programme deliberately left out piriformis and iliotibial band stretches. This is a precaution, not a tested harm: no trial tested stretching alone. The evidence also pulls the other way. Nava 2025 found a general programme with piriformis, abductor, adductor and iliotibial band stretches no worse on pain than motor control exercise, and Rompe 2009's home programme, which included piriformis and iliotibial band stretches, reached 80% success at 15 months. Neither isolates stretching or shows it is safe.

avoidOrModify.movement: Loaded exercise that takes the hip across the midline into adduction, or drops the pelvis on the working side
avoidOrModify.rationale: Keep the hip neutral or slightly abducted during loading. Hip adduction is proposed as a key mechanical factor, and the LEAP programme limited adduction in its exercises, but that restriction was not isolated from the rest of the programme.

avoidOrModify.movement: Heavy single-leg squats and similar single-leg sagittal-plane lifts
avoidOrModify.rationale: These are naturally performed in some hip adduction, so tendon compression cannot be avoided. Modelling in healthy young athletes places a loaded single-leg squat and a loaded single-leg Romanian deadlift among the highest gluteus medius and minimus loads tested. LEAP still progressed through single-leg-biased work, which supports graded use rather than exclusion.

avoidOrModify.movement: Lying on the painful side, or side-lying with the top leg resting across the body, during floor exercise or rest
avoidOrModify.rationale: Side-lying compresses the lower hip against the surface and adducts the upper hip. Place the painful side uppermost with pillows between the knees, or use a supine alternative. ISHA also advises sleeping supine with a pillow under the knees, or side-lying with a pillow between the legs.

avoidOrModify.movement: Clamshell exercise, with or without a band
avoidOrModify.rationale: One clinician fact sheet says it may be provocative through friction and compression at the greater trochanter. A fine-wire EMG study in 10 healthy adults also found it poor at recruiting gluteus medius. No trial shows that it harms people with this condition, and the motor control arm of Nava 2025 used it in weeks 1-2. Prefer another abductor exercise.

avoidOrModify.movement: Long-distance, tempo or hill running, plyometric drills and other rapid stretch-shortening work
avoidOrModify.rationale: High tensile loads, especially when increased quickly, are thought to aggravate tendon pain. Temporary suspension may be needed, while activity can usually continue in some form without its most provocative parts.

avoidOrModify.movement: Hill walking, stair climbing and long walks
avoidOrModify.rationale: For older or deconditioned people, the proposed approach is to limit hills and stairs and adjust walking distance to control symptoms. People with this condition show a greater hip adduction moment impulse on stair ascent than pain-free controls, and a greater hip adduction moment during walking stance than people with hip osteoarthritis, but those studies are cross-sectional and cannot show that stairs cause harm.

avoidOrModify.movement: Prolonged time balancing on one leg
avoidOrModify.rationale: The ISHA panel advises minimising single-leg time in daily activities, such as sitting to dress, to reduce tensile load. Its application to workout design is an extrapolation, and Nava's motor control programme prescribed 15 s single-leg holds from week 5.

avoidOrModify.movement: Hip abductor strengthening progressed quickly or performed through significant pain
avoidOrModify.rationale: Progress slowly, and treat pain that rises overnight or the next morning as a sign of too much load. LEAP used two pain rules: no change in pain over the greater trochanter during functional retraining, and up to 5/10 during heavy slow strengthening only if it eased afterwards and did not increase that night or the next morning. Load was adjusted to prevent week-to-week increases. Clifford 2019 and LEAP-Ireland used a similar 5/10 limit. These were programme rules chosen by trial authors, and Escriche-Escuder 2020 says pain-based progression is not supported by strong evidence. A narrative review is stricter, progressing only when pain-free. A commentary proposes starting at moderate effort and limiting high-load work to 3 times per week.

avoidOrModify.movement: Sitting or standing with the legs crossed or the hip hanging into adduction, including during rests and seated work
avoidOrModify.rationale: ISHA advises avoiding hip adduction in sitting, standing and sleeping, and avoiding crossed legs. Compression education of this type was part of the effective trial programmes, but no trial tested each restriction alone.

avoidOrModify.movement: Side plank and side-plank variations used as a beginner core exercise
avoidOrModify.rationale: In modelling of 14 healthy young female footballers, a bodyweight side plank was in the top tier for gluteus medius (338-483 N) and minimus (272-382 N) force. Treating it as a high-load exercise for this condition is an inference: the study measured no tendon compression and no harm, and it did not include people with this condition.

avoidOrModify.movement: Hard loading soon after a corticosteroid or platelet-rich plasma injection
avoidOrModify.rationale: ISHA advises starting with gentle isometrics, pain-free stretching that avoids compression through the lateral tendons, and neuromuscular control work, then adding eccentric abductor strengthening and dynamic single-leg work when tolerated. It advises longer rest after platelet-rich plasma than after corticosteroid, with no duration given.

dose.frequency: Daily, with 60 s rest between holds

candidateExercises.cautions: Keep pillows between the knees and do not let the top hip drop into adduction. redFlags.sign: Hip or groin pain that worsens with weight bearing after a fall or a rapid increase in activity, especially with known osteoporosis
redFlags.action: Stop the plan and seek prompt medical assessment for possible hip fracture

redFlags.sign: Hip or groin pain linked to repetitive weight-bearing exercise, particularly in endurance athletes, smokers, steroid users or people with female athlete triad
redFlags.action: Stop impact and loading work and seek medical assessment for possible stress fracture, since an early X-ray can be normal

redFlags.sign: Sudden hip pain without injury that makes weight bearing difficult, especially with diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, recent joint surgery, a prosthesis or age over 80
redFlags.action: Seek urgent medical assessment for possible joint infection

redFlags.sign: Deep, unrelenting pain, possibly worse at night, particularly with a history of cancer or unexplained weight loss
redFlags.action: Stop the plan and seek prompt medical assessment

redFlags.sign: Pain on walking with risk factors for osteonecrosis, including corticosteroid use, heavy alcohol use, smoking, lupus, sickle cell disease or HIV infection
redFlags.action: Seek medical assessment before continuing loading work

redFlags.sign: Heat, redness or swelling in several areas, morning stiffness over 1 hour, or symmetrical joint signs
redFlags.action: Seek medical assessment for possible inflammatory disease

redFlags.sign: Pain spreading below the knee, or lateral hip pain with low back pain
redFlags.action: Ask a clinician to check the back and leg, because the pain may not come from the gluteal tendons

redFlags.sign: Groin pain with morning stiffness, lost hip motion, locking, giving way, or difficulty putting on shoes and socks
redFlags.action: Ask a clinician to check for hip joint disease

redFlags.sign: Gluteal tendon repair surgery in the past 16 weeks
redFlags.action: Do not use this plan. Follow the surgical team's rehabilitation. ISHA's consensus limits hip flexion to 90 degrees, external rotation to 20 degrees and adduction to neutral in weeks 1-6, contraindicates active against-gravity abduction until week 8 and active long-lever hip flexion until week 12, and excludes jumping, hopping, cutting and pivoting in weeks 12-16.

redFlags.sign: A known gluteal tendon tear or rupture on imaging
redFlags.action: Ask a clinician before loading. Spencer 2026 found no non-surgical treatment studies for symptomatic tears. One later uncontrolled cohort reported no adverse events and no worse outcome in its rupture subgroup, which is too weak to establish safety.

limitations: Evidence grade stays low. Education plus exercise has the best support, but Bremer 2025's 'moderate' means findings from a single high-quality trial, Cordeiro 2024 rates certainty low to very low, a web search snippet gives Kjeldsen 2024 low-to-moderate certainty, and Slawaska-Eng 2025 reports a median continuous fragility index of 2 across 21 RCTs. No individual exercise is proven. Guidelines: no dedicated clinical practice guideline for this condition was found. The nearest documents are ISHA 2023 (Delphi consensus, no grades), Fearon 2024 (outcome measures only), NICE HTG248 (one procedure, 2011), ACR 2023 (imaging only, no GTPS-specific variant), Sconfienza 2022 and D'Souza 2024 (injections only) and two regional NHS documents. Enseki 2023 excludes extra-articular pain, so its graded recommendations should not be transferred. NICE CKS, the Cochrane Library, AAOS, WHO and national guideline libraries were not searched directly or could not be opened, so this is not an exhaustive negative. Cochrane: PubMed and Europe PMC filters found no review of this condition and one searcher found none on the Cochrane domain, but another domain search listed CD008924 (Bierma-Zeinstra 2011, 'Interventions for lateral hip pain'). Only its title and DOI could be confirmed, and the page returned HTTP 403, so a Cochrane record exists whose status and content are unknown. Contradictions. (1) Exercise ranking: Wang 2025 and Gazendam 2022 favour exercise for function or pain, while He 2023 ranks exercise lowest for VAS pain, behind shockwave and platelet-rich plasma, and Ladurner 2021 rates platelet-rich plasma above exercise, with one author's own trial in its evidence. (2) Added value of exercise: Ganderton 2018 and McMillan 2022 found targeted exercise no better than sham when both arms had education, and Mellor 2022 found strength did not mediate benefit, so education may be the active part. (3) Injection: LEAP favoured education plus exercise over injection at 8 and 52 weeks on global success, but Challoumas 2023 pooled short-term pain in favour of injection, Rompe 2009 found injection far ahead at 1 month, Cordeiro 2024 found no pain difference (I2 93-99%), and Nissen 2019 found injection no better than saline, although Sconfienza 2022 calls injection effective with 100% panel agreement. (4) Stretching: LEAP, NHS Lothian and Challoumas advise against it, but Nava 2025's general arm and Rompe 2009's home programme included these stretches with good results, none of which isolates stretching, and 53% of physiotherapists surveyed still used it (French 2020). (5) Eccentric work: ISHA progresses to eccentric loading, while Challoumas does not recommend eccentric loading alone. (6) Isometrics: Challoumas suggests them when isotonic loading is not tolerated, but Clifford 2019 and Clifford 2020 found no advantage. (7) Shockwave: Bremer 2025 prints a long-term SMD of 5.77 that is implausibly large and should not be used, Harding 2024 found no significant effect against control, Wheeler 2022 found no benefit over minimal dose, and 7 of 8 RCTs in Rhim 2024 were at high risk of bias. NICE allows it only under special arrangements. (8) Recovery rates: ISHA gives 60-90%, NHS Lothian over 90%, LEAP 77-78% global success, and Hogsholt 2026 only 37% in MRI-verified disease. (9) Surgery and tears: NHS Lothian says surgery is rarely if ever needed, while ISHA says some patients may require it and Ladurner 2021 gives repair its top symbol at LoE 4. Spencer 2026 found no non-surgical evidence for tears, and Hogsholt 2026, published later, reported a rupture subgroup without a control. (10) Pain rule: trials allowed up to 5/10, while Gonzalez-de-la-Flor 2025 advises progressing only without pain. (11) EMG: Collings 2025 found poor agreement between EMG and force rankings (rho 0.29-0.51), so EMG-based rankings such as Moore 2020 and Ebert 2017 should not set load order. Compression and stretching advice rests on expert reasoning and has not been tested alone. No study found measures tendon compression during gym exercises, and Collings 2023 and Wang S 2025 are healthy-person models. Participants were mostly women, many postmenopausal. LEAP excluded back, sciatic or groin pain above 2/10 and total hip replacement. LEAP also included supervised sessions with specialised equipment; the sliding platform work is omitted here. Doses come from multi-part or pilot programmes and are not validated as stand-alone prescriptions. Table values in the LEAP protocol are offset in XML, and 'Hold 15s' with '8-12' in the Nava protocol is ambiguous. Printed errors to avoid quoting: Challoumas's long-term estimate, Cordeiro's Rompe arm sizes and participant totals. Ganderton 2018 and McMillan 2022 doses are available only through Cordeiro 2024's table. Red-flag action wording was written for this app, because no source provides a red-flag list specific to this condition; the York pathway lists its red flags as 'None provided'. Reading depth is in each source's accessLevel. Abstract-only sources gave no adverse event detail in most cases, full-text sources were often read by targeted extraction, and LEAP's per-arm non-serious adverse events sit in an unopened web appendix. Grimaldi and Fearon 2015 and Wilson and Furukawa 2014, which carry most red flags, were reopened and read by targeted extraction. Moore 2019 and Ganderton 2017 were checked at abstract level. None of this is treatment advice.

valuesCorrected: Hill walking row: Allison 2016 compared stair ascent with pain-free controls, and Allison 2018 compared walking with hip osteoarthritis, not controls, and reports the moment rather than its impulse. Wording corrected.
Side-lying row: ISHA gives supine with a pillow under the knees or side-lying with a pillow between the legs. The second option had been dropped.
accessLevel: grimaldi_fearon_2015 and wilson_furukawa_2014 from not_reconfirmed to full_text; moore_gmed_2019 and ganderton_2017 from not_reconfirmed to abstract_only.

bierma_zeinstra_2011: type trial_registry to cochrane_record. Crossref lists it as a Cochrane item, not a registry entry.
unverifiable: Kjeldsen 2024: the low-to-moderate certainty rating comes from a web snippet. The abstract does not state it, and the full text was not opened.
CD008924: title, authors and date confirmed through Crossref only, so its content and whether it is a review or a protocol are unknown.
LEAP Table 3 was read as flattened text, not the published layout, so the supine and standing isometric doses remain a reading of row order. BD is defined only as bi-daily.
Nava's 'Hold 15s' with '8-12' cell states no rule for combining them.
French 2020: the 53% stretching figure was confirmed from a search summary of the abstract, with no denominator.
Grimaldi and Fearon 2015 was read from a third-party PDF copy on wikiMSK, and its figures were not viewed.
Full-text sources were checked by targeted extraction, not read end to end. LEAP non-serious adverse events remain in an unopened appendix.
